subject: curve-fitting problems: exposing functions from the function block

messages.author: 4ccd18c0da758c60
messages.subject: curve-fitting problems: exposing functions from the function block
parts:
Hi, 

I am doing a fairly straightforward nonlinear curve-fitting problem with independent Gaussian errors. I have set it up in pystan and am pretty happy with the results. (For the aficionados, I am fitting sub-millimetre galaxy spectral energy distributions.)

One nice way to visualise the results is to actually show the "best-fit" curve (or, better, various samples from the posterior), but at many more x values (in my case, observed wavelengths) than the small number where I have actual data.

However, in order to do that, I basically need to recode the model in python and use matplotlib to make the curve using the parameters that I get from the get_posterior_mean() method (and/or from a subset of the posterior samples if I'm doing more serious model checking).

I could probably do some of this within Stan using "generated quantities" but this would require a large number of these (for each of the x values) which would be inefficient and difficult to play with interactively.

A simple solution to this problem would be to write the fitting function in the actual function block (although this isn't currently how I have the code structured) and expose this to python. As of now, definitions in the function block is only available within Stan, but I imagine it should be possible to make them available (as the various log_probabilty functions are). Any chance of this happening?

Yours,

Andrew

There is an expose_stan_functions() that does exactly this in the rstan R package. It isn't currently available in pystan or any other interface to Stan.

Ben

Let's be a little more encouraging---the expose_stan_functions function leverages Rcpp a little bit to do this,  but I think most of it was regex magic that should be obvious from the function.  Or, simply process your .stan function with R's expose_stan_functions() and then look up the .cpp file it compiles (somewhere in your temp directory).  At that point the hard part is figuring out how to compile it and expose it to Python, not really a Stan-related task and totally doable.  Krzysztof
